items.prompt: Finish the simile: as quiet as a ___.

options.text: mouse
lion
options.why: Lions roar. They are known for being loud.

options.text: drum
options.why: Drums are loud.

options.text: storm
options.why: Storms are noisy.

hints: A simile compares two things using like or as.
Think of a small animal that makes almost no sound.
Which of these would you hardly hear?
items.explanation: The simile is as quiet as a mouse, because mice are small and make very little noise.

items.prompt: Which sentence has a simile?

options.text: The cat is black.
options.why: This describes the cat, but it does not compare it to anything.

options.text: The cat sleeps a lot.
options.why: There is no comparison here.

options.text: The cat is as black as coal.
My cat is called Coal.
options.why: This is the cat's name, not a comparison.

hints: A simile compares one thing to another.
Look for the words like or as.
Which sentence says the cat is like something else?
items.explanation: As black as coal compares the cat's colour to coal, using as. That makes it a simile.

items.prompt: Match the simile beginnings to their endings.
hints: Each simile compares something to a thing that is famous for that quality.
Which thing is very light? Which is very slow?
Start with as cold as. What is the coldest thing in the list?
items.explanation: These similes compare a quality to something well known for it: a feather is light and a snail is slow.

items.prompt:
Which two things are being compared?
The moon was like a silver coin.

options.text: the moon and the sky
options.why: The sky is not in this sentence.

options.text: silver and gold
options.why: Gold is not mentioned.

options.text: a coin and a purse
options.why: A purse is not mentioned.

options.text: the moon and a coin

hints: Find the word like.
What comes before like? What comes after it?
Those are the two things being compared.
items.explanation: The word like compares the moon with a silver coin, because both are round and shiny.

items.prompt: Choose 2 sentences that contain a simile.

options.text: Her hands were as cold as ice.
The road was long and dusty.
options.why: This describes the road, but it does not compare it.

options.text: He ran like the wind.
I like mangoes.
options.why: Here like means enjoy. Nothing is being compared.

options.text: The river was wide.
options.why: There is no comparison here.

hints: A simile compares two things with like or as.
Careful: like can also mean enjoy.
Check each sentence. Is one thing being compared to another?
items.explanation: As cold as ice and like the wind are similes. In I like mangoes, like means enjoy, so it is not a simile.

items.prompt: What does as quick as a flash mean?

options.text: very bright
options.why: A flash is bright, but this simile is about speed.

options.text: very fast
very loud
options.why: This simile is about speed, not sound.

options.text: very slowly
options.why: It means the opposite of slowly.

hints: Look at the word quick.
A flash of light lasts for a tiny moment.
So what is the simile really telling you?
items.explanation: A flash happens in an instant, so as quick as a flash means very fast.

items.prompt: Which simile best describes a very hot day?

options.text: The air was as hot as an oven.
The air was as cool as a cucumber.
options.why: Cool is the opposite of hot.

options.text: The air was as fresh as a daisy.
options.why: Fresh does not describe heat.

options.text: The air was like a soft feather.
options.why: A feather is soft and light, not hot.

hints: You need a simile about heat.
Think of something in the kitchen that is very hot.
Cross out the similes that are about something else.
items.explanation: An oven is very hot, so as hot as an oven describes a very hot day.

items.prompt: Sort the phrases: simile or not a simile?
hints: A simile compares two things.
Look for as ... as, or like used to compare.
Like can also mean enjoy. Check how it is used.
items.explanation: Similes compare, like as white as snow. I like cats and she likes to sing use like to mean enjoy, so they are not similes.

items.prompt: The children's voices buzzed like bees in the classroom. Why did the writer use this simile?

options.text: to show that there were bees in the room
options.why: There were no real bees. The voices only sounded like bees.

options.text: to show that the children were scared
options.why: Buzzing bees suggest busy noise, not fear.

options.text: to show that the room was noisy and busy
to show that it was very quiet
options.why: Buzzing is a noisy sound.

hints: Think about the sound a group of bees makes.
Is it loud or quiet? Is it calm or busy?
Now picture a classroom that sounds like that.
items.explanation: Bees make a busy humming noise. The simile shows the classroom was full of busy, noisy chatter.

items.prompt: Choose the best simile to show that Lina was very nervous.

options.text: Lina was as happy as a lark.
options.why: This shows happiness, not nerves.

options.text: Lina ran like a cheetah.
options.why: This shows speed, not nerves.

options.text: Lina's legs were long.
options.why: This is not a simile.

options.text: Lina's legs felt like jelly.

hints: Think about how your body feels when you are nervous.
When you are nervous, your knees may feel weak and wobbly.
Which simile compares Lina's body to something wobbly?
items.explanation: Legs that feel like jelly are wobbly and weak. This simile shows that Lina was very nervous.

items.prompt: Which sentence is NOT a simile?

options.text: The clouds were like cotton wool.
options.why: This compares clouds to cotton wool using like.

options.text: The lake was as flat as a mirror.
options.why: This compares the lake to a mirror using as.

options.text: The wind howled all night.
Her smile was as bright as the sun.
options.why: This compares a smile to the sun using as.

hints: Three of the sentences compare two things.
Look for like or as in each sentence.
Which sentence describes something without comparing it?
items.explanation: The wind howled all night describes the wind, but it does not compare it to anything with like or as.

items.prompt: The old bridge creaked and groaned like a ship in a storm. What does this simile suggest about the bridge?

options.text: It was new and strong.
options.why: Creaking and groaning suggest it is old and under strain.

options.text: It was old and not very steady.
It was floating on water.
options.why: The bridge is compared to a ship's sound, not its place.

options.text: It was painted like a ship.
options.why: The simile is about the sound, not the colour.

hints: Think about the sounds a ship makes in a storm.
Creaking and groaning are the sounds of wood under strain.
How might you feel walking across this bridge?
items.explanation: A ship in a storm creaks because it is pushed and strained. The simile suggests the bridge is old and not very steady.

items.prompt:
Choose the best word to finish the simile.
Her smile was as bright as the ___.
hints: A simile compares two things.
Which of these things is very bright?
Say each choice in the sentence and listen.
items.explanation: A smile and the sun are both bright. So as bright as the sun makes a clear simile.

items.prompt:
Which word shows a simile?
The snow was like a soft white blanket.

options.text: was
options.why: Was is a verb. It does not compare two things.

options.text: like
soft
options.why: Soft describes the blanket. It does not make the comparison.

options.text: white
options.why: White describes the colour. It does not make the comparison.

hints: A simile uses a small word to compare.
The two words are like and as.
Which of these is one of them?
items.explanation: Like joins the snow to a blanket. It is the word that makes the comparison.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to make a simile.
items.answer: The baby was as quiet as a mouse.
hints: A simile with as needs as twice.
The pattern is as (describing word) as a (thing).
Start with The baby was.
items.explanation: As quiet as a mouse compares the baby to a quiet animal. It uses as twice.

items.prompt:
Write like or as in each gap.
The clouds floated ___ cotton wool across the sky. Tom was ___ tall as a tree.
hints: One gap needs a word that stands alone. The other makes a pair with as.
The second gap has as tall as, so the first half needs as.
In the first sentence, there is no second as later on.
items.explanation: The clouds floated like cotton wool uses like. Tom was as tall as a tree uses as ... as.

items.prompt: Match each simile beginning to the best ending.
hints: Think about what each thing is famous for.
Do the easiest one first.
Giraffes and honey are both clear. Start there.
items.explanation: Each ending is something known for that quality: sweet honey, flat pancake, tall giraffe, tough leather.

items.prompt:
Dewi's laugh rang out like a bell.
What does this simile tell us?

options.text: Her laugh was sad and slow.
options.why: A bell ringing is clear and bright, not sad and slow.

options.text: Her laugh was clear and cheerful.
Her laugh was very quiet.
options.why: A ringing bell is loud and clear, not quiet.

options.text: Her laugh made a sound like metal breaking.
options.why: The comparison is about a clear, pleasant sound, not a broken one.

hints: Think about the sound of a bell.
A bell rings clearly. Is it a happy or sad sound here?
Look at the verb rang out.
items.explanation: A bell rings clearly and brightly. So Dewi's laugh was clear and cheerful.

items.prompt: Which simile best shows a very crowded bus?

options.text: The bus was as empty as a bowl.
options.why: Empty means nobody is on it, which is the opposite.

options.text: The bus was as quiet as a library.
options.why: This tells us about noise, not about people.

options.text: The bus was as packed as a tin of sardines.
The bus was as clean as a whistle.
options.why: This tells us about cleanliness, not how crowded it is.

hints: Decide what the simile must show: lots of people.
Which thing is full to the top with things squeezed together?
Cross out the ones about noise and cleaning.
items.explanation: Sardines are squeezed tightly in a tin, just like people on a crowded bus.

items.prompt: Sort the similes. Do they describe speed or loudness?
hints: Think about what each comparison makes you picture.
Hares and blinks are quick. Thunder and drums are loud.
Start with as loud as thunder.
items.explanation: Lightning, a hare and a blink are all quick. A drum, thunder and a roaring engine are all loud.

items.prompt:
Choose the right word for each gap.
Yuki waited at the door, her heart thumping ___ a drum. The hallway was as dark ___ a cave.
hints: A simile uses either like or as ... as.
Look for the first as in the second sentence.
Is there an as before the gap in the second sentence? That helps you.
items.explanation: Thumping like a drum uses like. As dark as a cave uses as twice.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to make a simile.
items.answer: His hands were as rough as bark.
hints: Find the two as words first.
The thing being described comes first: His hands.
Rough is what the hands are like. Bark is what they are compared to.
items.explanation: His hands are compared to bark to show they were rough.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows best that the cake was very sweet?

options.text: The cake was very very sweet.
options.why: This repeats very, but it does not make a picture with a comparison.

options.text: The cake was as sweet as syrup poured on honey.
The cake was sweet, and it was a cake.
options.why: This does not add anything new about the cake.

options.text: The cake was not bitter.
options.why: This tells us what it was not, but does not show the sweetness.

hints: A simile gives a clearer picture than just saying very.
Look for the sentence that compares the cake to something sweet.
Which option has as ... as or like?
items.explanation: A simile compares the cake to something very sweet. It makes a stronger picture than very very.

items.prompt:
Read.
The storm began slowly. Rain tapped on the roof like tiny fingers. Then it thundered down like a herd of buffalo.
What does the second simile suggest?

options.text: The rain became softer.
options.why: Tiny fingers was the soft one. The herd of buffalo is the opposite.

options.text: The rain stopped.
options.why: A herd of buffalo is loud and strong, so the rain did not stop.

options.text: The rain became heavy and loud.
The rain was cold.
options.why: The simile is about weight and noise, not temperature.

hints: Compare the two similes in the paragraph.
Tiny fingers is soft. What is a herd of buffalo like?
Think of heavy feet making noise.
items.explanation: A herd of buffalo is heavy and noisy. So the rain went from light tapping to heavy pounding.

items.prompt: The writer is describing a calm lake. Which simile does NOT fit?

options.text: The lake was as smooth as glass.
options.why: This fits. Glass is smooth and flat, like a calm lake.

options.text: The lake was as still as a photograph.
options.why: This fits. A photograph does not move, like calm water.

options.text: The lake was as wild as a stormy sea.
The water was as quiet as a feather falling.
options.why: This fits. A falling feather makes no sound, like calm water.

hints: Look for the one that is the opposite of calm.
Which comparison is about waves and wind?
Cross out each simile that matches smooth, still or quiet.
items.explanation: A stormy sea is rough and wild, the opposite of a calm lake. So it does not fit.

items.prompt:
The teacher's voice was like sandpaper.
What does this tell us?

options.text: It was soft and warm.
options.why: Sandpaper is rough, not soft and warm.

options.text: It was cheerful and light.
options.why: Sandpaper is not a cheerful thing. It feels harsh.

options.text: It was rough and harsh.
It was loud and fast.
options.why: Sandpaper is about how something feels, not how loud or fast it is.

hints: Think about how sandpaper feels on your hand.
A voice cannot feel rough, so the writer means the sound is rough.
Choose the words that match sandpaper.
items.explanation: Sandpaper is rough. The simile suggests the voice sounded rough and harsh.

items.prompt: Which sentence is NOT a simile?

options.text: The runner was as quick as a train.
options.why: This compares a runner to a train, which are different things. It is a simile.

options.text: Tom is as tall as his brother.
The moon hung like a lantern above the hill.
options.why: This compares the moon to a lantern. It is a simile.

options.text: She moved like a shadow along the wall.
options.why: This compares her movement to a shadow. It is a simile.

hints: A simile compares two different things.
Check what is being compared in each sentence.
Which sentence compares two things of the same kind?
items.explanation: Tom and his brother are the same kind of thing, two boys. A simile compares things that are different.

items.prompt: Choose 2 similes that show a character is shy.

options.text: He marched in like a king.
options.why: This shows confidence, the opposite of shy.

options.text: She hid behind her mum like a shadow.
He roared with laughter like a lion.
options.why: This shows loud and bold, not shy.

options.text: Her voice was as small as a whisper.
The class was as busy as a hive.
options.why: This is about a busy class, not a shy person.

hints: Shy means quiet and nervous around others.
Which comparisons are about being small, quiet or hidden?
Cross out the bold and loud ones first.
items.explanation: A shadow follows quietly behind someone, and a whisper is small and soft. Both show shyness.
